items.title: Space Lasers Are Fast, But Clouds Still Rule the Forecast
items.summary: Since the launch of Sputnik, humanity has talked to its spacecraft through radio waves. Radio is great for communication through any weather, but it has hit a limit – traditional radio frequencies are highly regulated by bodies like the International Telecommunications Union, which limits the scalability of radio communications networks to meet the growing demand of bandwidth to and from space. The obvious solution is to switch to infrared lasers, which have an extremely high data transfer rate. However, according to a paper available in pre-print on arXiv from Dr. Slava Turyshev – best known to UT readers for his work on turning the Sun’s gravity into a giant telescope – the raw speed of laser communication isn’t the bottleneck, it’s the system’s reliability.
items.t: Space Lasers Are Fast, But Clouds Still Rule the Forecast

Astronomy Picture of the Day

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. 

Galaxies Battle in the NGC 7771 Group 

Explanation: After this galaxy battle, only one galaxy will remain. Already visible in the featured picture are rings and faint star swirls from previous gravitational encounters . Known collectively as the NGC 7771 Group , these galaxies lie almost 200 million light-years away toward the high-flying constellation Pegasus . The largest galaxy, barred spiral NGC 7771 on the lower right, is itself about 75,000 light-years across, and the galaxy on the upper left is spiral NGC 7769 , which is almost as large. As these and other smaller galaxies make repeated close passages, they will all likely merge into one very large galaxy. Playing out over billions of years, the merger process is understood to be a normal part of the evolution of galaxies . Studying galaxy clashes like this helps humanity to better understand the possible merger between our own Milky Way and Andromeda galaxies.

items.title: NASA Awards Contract for NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network Program
items.summary:
Credit: NASA 

NASA, on behalf of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), has awarded a contract to Northrop Grumman Systems Corporation for the Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA) instruments on NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) satellites.

The cost-plus-fixed-fee, firm-fixed-price, and time-and-materials hybrid contract has a value of $290.6 million. The period of performance runs from Nov. 23 through April 1, 2042. The work will take place at the awardee’s facility.

Under the contract, Northrop Grumman will provide the design, development, production, testing, and mission support for three SMBA instruments, the next generation of low Earth orbit microwave sounders. NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, is managing the acquisition, and NOAA will own and operate the instruments and deliver the data to users worldwide. Microwave sounders provide critical measurements of temperature and moisture in the atmosphere, which significantly influence weather patterns. The SMBA instruments could improve the medium-range forecasts for NOAA’s National Weather Service.

The NEON mission is a collaboration between NASA and NOAA. The mission is led by NOAA, which provides funding, technical requirements, and postlaunch operations. NASA will manage the development of the NEON satellites and launch them for NOAA. NASA and NOAA will work with commercial partners to design and build the NEON spacecraft and instruments.

For information about NASA and agency programs, visit:

https://www.nasa.gov

items.title: Detecting Primordial Black Holes By The Stars They Destroy
items.summary: Astrophysicists wonder if primordial black holes could be part, or maybe all, of dark matter. They're theorized to have formed immediately after the Big Bang from pockets of dense matter. New research shows how they might be detected: in the bbright flash generated by the stars they consume from the inside out.

items.title: Ultra-Thin "Rainbow" Sails Could Power Spacecraft and Shade the Earth
items.summary: For years, whimsically minded space enthusiasts have been dreaming of sailing across the vastness of the void on beams of sunlight. Photons, the massless particles that make up those beams of sunlight, still carry momentum, and can therefore impart a gentle push when they bounce off a surface. This force is the concept behind “solar sailing”, which has been having a bit of a moment in the last decade as several proof-of-concept flights have shown it is indeed actually feasible. Now a new paper, available in pre-print on arXiv from researchers at the Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT), has unveiled a clever technique that will allow these giant sails to steer sideways using a technology more commonly associated with flat-screen displays.
items.t: Ultra-Thin "Rainbow" Sails Could Power Spacecraft and Shade the Earth

items.title: Studying Cancer Cells in Microgravity
items.summary:
Encapsulate Inc. 

This Nov. 19, 2026, image shows gastric microtumors grown within an Encapsulates biochip. The Encapsulate-1 investigation studies patient-derived tumor samples aboard the International Space Station to better understand how cancer cells move and interact in microgravity. The results could help researchers develop further testing to predict a patient’s risk of metastasis and support more personalized cancer treatments.

Orbiting more than 200 miles (320 km) above Earth, the space station is a powerhouse of cutting-edge science that is unlocking discoveries not possible on Earth.

items.title: NASA Seeks Partners to Design First Nuclear Reactor for the Moon
items.summary:
Artist’s concept of a nuclear fission power system on the Moon’s surface. Credit: NASA 

NASA is seeking industry partners to develop and test the first nuclear reactor designed to provide electricity on the Moon, a major step toward establishing a sustained human presence on the lunar surface. 

Lunar Reactor-1 (LR-1) will be a small fission power system that will generate 20 kilowatts of electricity, enough to power approximately 16 average U.S. households annually on Earth. For NASA’s plans for a Moon Base , that energy could support future habitats, communications systems, rovers, scientific instruments, and other essential infrastructure. 

NASA aims to have a launch-ready system by 2030 and operate it on the Moon for at least five years after deployment. 

Unlike solar power, which depends on sunlight, a nuclear reactor can generate electricity continuously, including during the Moon’s approximately two-week-long nights. This capability will enable future lunar operations, particularly in locations where sunlight is limited or unavailable. 

“This request for proposals represents an important step forward as NASA partners with industry to establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface,” said Brian Giblin, NASA’s Lunar Reactor-1 program manager. “A reliable source of safe and abundant energy will be vital to future exploration of the lunar and Martian surface. Space nuclear systems will provide continuous power to NASA assets in any environment without dependency on sunlight.”

items.t: NASA Seeks Partners to Design First Nuclear Reactor for the Moon

items.title: LISA's Gravitational Wave Detections Could Reveal Exoplanets
items.summary: LISA, the ESA's Laser Interferometry Space Antenna, is being built to detect gravitational waves emitted when massive objects spiral together and merge. New research shows that exoplanets can exert a small but perceptible tug on those objects, leaving a signature on the gravitational waves. In some cases, LISA should be able to detect their signatures.

items.title: NASA+ Documentary Captures Europa Clipper’s Journey Into Deep Space
items.summary:
4 min read

Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) 

The NASA+ original documentary “The Europa Concept” takes audiences along on the journey to send a spacecraft to Jupiter’s moon Europa to determine whether the ocean beneath the moon’s icy shell has the ingredients for life. 
Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech 

NASA invites the world behind the scenes to witness the story of Europa Clipper’s journey from a far-off vision to a cutting-edge deep space exploration mission with the release of the agency’s newest documentary, “The Europa Concept.”

The documentary will air on NASA+ , the NASA app, and the agency’s website starting Monday, Nov. 23, and is coming soon to YouTube.

It took decades of science, thousands of dedicated minds, endless creativity, and a whole lot of grit to get the Europa Clipper spacecraft to the launch pad in 2024. Now the orbiter, the largest NASA has ever sent into deep space, is two years into its five-year, 1.8 billion-mile (2.9 billion-kilometer) journey to the Jupiter system, where it will conduct flybys of Europa in search of the conditions for life in the vast ocean thought to hide beneath the moon’s icy surface.

“The things we will learn from Europa Clipper will be so sensational, so fantastic, that everyone will be screaming for the next mission,” said Curt Niebur, program scientist in the Planetary Science Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “The only thing that matters is that we learn enough that we, in the broadest sense, want to do it again somewhere else — because that’s what exploration is.”

items.title: Bacteria and Nuclear Power Could Grow Ready-Made Homes on Mars Before Astronauts Arrive
items.summary: As we gear up to eventually land a human on Mars, more and more ideas are coming out about how to prepare for that. A recent one from Pioneer Labs, a research institute founded by bioengineer Erika DeBenedictis to develop biological technologies for space exploration, is now available on arXiv, without any plans to release it in a paid journal as part of the “Open Science” policy of The Astera Institute, who funded the research. It details “Mars Seed” - a new architecture that is self-contained and can produce a full 870 sq meters of pressurized habitat using nothing but Martian inputs within roughly every four Earth years.
items.t: Bacteria and Nuclear Power Could Grow Ready-Made Homes on Mars Before Astronauts Arrive

Astronomy Picture of the Day

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. 

The Emergence of Dark Nebula Lynds 1251 

Explanation: If you stare into space for a long time, what might you see? At first, you might only see the usual brightest stars , but if your eyes (or camera) could continue to collect light , you would see increasingly more. In the direction of the featured image , after only a few minutes, you would begin to notice some regions without stars . As your staring continued, the dark region would become better defined, and after a full 20 hours, you would notice a strange dark structure . To celebrate, you use digital processing to brighten the image and enhance the colors. At the end, you might have an excellent image of Lynds 1251 (LDN 1251), a star -forming region laced with opaque brown-appearing interstellar dust. Also known as the Rotten Fish Nebula, LDN 1251 is home not only to young stars and dust , but also, your long staring indicates, energetic shock waves , fast stellar winds , and powerfully beamed jets .

 NASA Earth Observatory/Lauren Dauphin 

More than 60 years ago, scientists at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center aimed a laser skyward and fired a pulse of light at an orbiting satellite equipped with special reflectors. By measuring the time it took for the light to return, they demonstrated a new, more precise method for tracking satellites.

Since then, satellite laser ranging (SLR) has grown more precise and more widely used. The technique now underpins many aspects of Earth observation, such as validating satellite orbits and mapping subtle changes to Earth’s surface. Pioneered at the Goddard Optical Research Facility—now the Goddard Geophysical and Astronomical Observatory —laser ranging is performed at more than 40 stations worldwide.

items.t: Space Entrepreneurs Should Look To 16th Century Spice Trade For Inspiration

items.title: Complex Life on Earth May Not Have Appeared Without Tall Mountains
items.summary: As Earth's surface area grew, weathering fed more nutrients into Earth's ancient oceans. This eventually resulted in more oxygen, making Earth more habitable. New research identifies two ancient mountain growth spurts on Earth that directly preceded two of Earth's oxygenation events. The researchers say that taller mountains encouraged habitability and led to complex life.
items.t: Complex Life on Earth May Not Have Appeared Without Tall Mountains

items.title: A Radical Theory about the Universe Just Passed Some Key Tests. So... What Does that Mean?
items.summary: An alternative model in which the Universe is 26.7 billion years old and needs neither dark matter nor dark energy has held up against several major cosmology tests, according to a new University of Ottawa study.
items.t: A Radical Theory about the Universe Just Passed Some Key Tests. So... What Does that Mean?

items.title: A Triple Star System 'That Shouldn't Exist,' Only 28 Light-Years from Earth
items.summary: Astronomers have found a triple star system in our neighborhood that has defied the odds. It shouldn't really exist, according to astronomers' understanding of stellar evolution and common envelopes. Yet, there it is.
items.t: A Triple Star System 'That Shouldn't Exist,' Only 28 Light-Years from Earth

items.title: Sound Waves From Sunspots Launch Fiery Plasma Jets Across the Sun
items.summary: It feels like every week for the past few months we’ve been reporting on more research regarding the temperature difference between the Sun’s surface and its corona. This week is no exception, with a new paper in The Astrophysical Journal detailing the formation and tracking of around two hundred jet-like bursts of plasma from the surface known as “dynamic fibrils.” They serve as another piece of the puzzle of why the Sun’s outer atmosphere is hundreds of times hotter than its surface.
items.t: Sound Waves From Sunspots Launch Fiery Plasma Jets Across the Sun

items.title: This is the First Time Astronomers Have Seen One of These Stellar Mergers
items.summary: Some binary stars end up sharing a common envelope of gas, as the primary star draws material away from its companion. The envelope exerts drag on the stars and they can spiral toward each other. In some cases, this creates an eruption or explosion called a luminous red nova. For the first time, astronomers got to observe one of these in real time.
items.t: This is the First Time Astronomers Have Seen One of These Stellar Mergers

items.title: Tiny Grains of Sand Act as Cosmic Speedometers for Alien Winds
items.summary: We’ve managed to take high-resolution orbital images of many worlds across our solar system, and many of them with an atmosphere have one feature in common - sand dunes. Scientists have been using the size and orientation of these dunes for decades to act like a weather vane, figuring out which way the wind blows on these other worlds. Unfortunately, weather vanes aren’t good at telling the full windy story - they can’t tell you how fast the wind is going. However, according to a new paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences by researchers at Stanford, sand dunes can.
items.t: Tiny Grains of Sand Act as Cosmic Speedometers for Alien Winds

items.title: Earth's Atmosphere Took Three Deep Breaths of Oxygen Before the Oceans Caught Up
items.summary: The accumulation of oxygen in Earth's atmosphere and oceans was a multi-stage process that played out over geologic timescales. Scientists have worked hard to understand all the details of this complex process. New research writes a revised timeline for how it all played out.
items.t: Earth's Atmosphere Took Three Deep Breaths of Oxygen Before the Oceans Caught Up
